title: Intraoral radiographs: bitewing, periapical & occlusal
blurb: The three intraoral views, what each one shows, how they are taken and how to tell them apart at a glance.
question: The dentist asks you to prepare for two radiographs: one to check for decay between the back teeth, and one to look for an abscess at the root tip of a painful lower molar. Which views are needed, and how will the two images look different?

teach.body: An intraoral radiograph is taken with the receptor (film, phosphor plate or digital sensor) inside the patient's mouth. There are three main views. A bitewing shows the crowns of the upper and lower back teeth together. A periapical shows one or two whole teeth from crown to root tip, with the bone around the apex. An occlusal uses a larger receptor laid flat between the teeth to show a wide area of one jaw. Each answers a different clinical question.

teach.h: The three views at a glance

teach.caption: Upper and lower premolar and molar crowns on one image, with no root apices. Note the bright white (radiopaque) filling, and a carious lesion highlighted in red in an upper tooth.

teach.h: Teeth covered by a pair of bitewings
teach.caption: Bitewings are usually taken as a left and right pair, covering the premolars and molars of both jaws. They are the best view for decay between the teeth (interproximal caries), overhanging fillings and the crest of the bone. Turning the receptor upright (a vertical bitewing) shows more bone for periodontal assessment.

teach.body: A periapical must show the whole tooth, including the full root and apex, plus the surrounding bone, so the dentist can see apical infection, root shape, fractures or bone loss. UK guidance says the paralleling technique should be used whenever possible. The receptor sits in a holder parallel to the long axis of the tooth, and the beam is aimed at right angles to both using a beam-aiming device. This gives a more accurate, reproducible image at a lower dose than the older bisecting angle technique.

teach.h: A periapical of upper posterior teeth
teach.caption: Upper back teeth with their roots running up into the surrounding bone. Showing the roots and the bone around them, rather than the crowns of both jaws, is what tells a periapical apart from a bitewing.

teach.body: For an occlusal, a larger receptor is placed flat between the biting surfaces and the patient closes gently on it. It only covers one arch. An upper standard occlusal shows the front of the maxilla, for example unerupted canines or extra (supernumerary) teeth. A lower true occlusal has the beam aimed up through the floor of the mouth from under the chin, which shows stones in the submandibular duct, foreign bodies, and any swelling of the jaw towards the cheek or tongue.

teach.caption: The whole lower arch seen from below, with a rounded radiopaque object in the floor of the mouth, the kind of finding (such as a salivary stone) this view is used to look for.

teach.text: Quick test: can you see the root tips? If NO and both jaws are on the image, it's a bitewing. If YES and only one jaw, it's a periapical. Bitewings can't diagnose apical infection.

items: Bitewing: upper and lower posterior crowns, no apices; interproximal caries and crestal bone.
Vertical bitewing: more bone shown, for periodontal assessment.
Periapical: whole tooth and apex; paralleling technique with a holder is preferred.
Occlusal: receptor flat between the teeth, one arch; lower true occlusal for floor-of-mouth stones.

summary: You can now name the three intraoral views, say what each shows and is used for, explain the paralleling technique, describe how a bitewing is taken, and tell a bitewing from a periapical at a glance by looking for the apices.

A.q: The dentist wants to check for decay between the upper and lower back teeth on both sides. Which radiographs are most appropriate?
A.why: Bitewings show the crowns of the upper and lower premolars and molars together, ideal for interproximal caries.

whyNot.0: Periapicals show one or two whole teeth in one jaw, so they're not the first choice for caries screening.
whyNot.2: An upper occlusal shows the anterior maxilla, not the contacts between back teeth.
whyNot.3: A lower true occlusal shows the floor of the mouth, not interproximal surfaces.

A.q: Which feature confirms that a radiograph is a periapical rather than a bitewing?
A.why: A periapical shows the whole tooth including the apex and surrounding bone; bitewings never show the apices.

whyNot.0: Both jaws on one image is a feature of a bitewing.
whyNot.1: Fillings look radiopaque (white) on any radiograph.
whyNot.3: Crowns are visible on both bitewings and periapicals.

A.q: A patient has swelling under the tongue and the dentist suspects a stone in the submandibular duct. Which view is most useful?
A.why: A lower true occlusal aims the beam up through the floor of the mouth, showing submandibular duct stones.

whyNot.0: Bitewings show tooth crowns, not the floor of the mouth.
whyNot.1: A vertical bitewing shows periodontal bone levels, not soft tissue below the tongue.
whyNot.2: A periapical covers the teeth and apical bone, not the floor of the mouth.

B.q: Which technique is recommended for periapical radiographs in UK guidance?
B.why: Paralleling, with the receptor in a holder parallel to the tooth, gives better images, reproducibility and a lower dose.

whyNot.1: Bisecting angle is only used when paralleling isn't possible, such as under general anaesthetic.
whyNot.2: Free-hand positioning without holders increases errors and retakes.
whyNot.3: Panoramic is an extraoral view, not a periapical technique.

B.q: The dentist wants to assess periodontal bone levels around the back teeth. Which intraoral view shows more of the bone?
B.why: Turning the bitewing receptor upright shows more of the alveolar bone, which helps periodontal assessment.

whyNot.0: A horizontal bitewing shows crowns and bone crest but less bone height.
whyNot.1: An upper occlusal shows the anterior maxilla, not posterior bone levels.
whyNot.3: A lower true occlusal looks up through the floor of the mouth, not at bone levels.

B.q: When taking a bitewing, how should the X-ray beam be aimed?
options: Down the long axis of the tooth
Up through the floor of the mouth
Along the occlusal plane from behind
B.why: The beam passes through the contact points at right angles to the receptor so the contacts are open, not overlapped.

whyNot.0: Aiming down the long axis would not produce a bitewing image.
whyNot.2: Aiming up through the floor of the mouth is the lower true occlusal.
whyNot.3: This direction would not show the interproximal surfaces.

C.q: Why can't a bitewing be used to diagnose an abscess at the root tip?
options: It is too low a dose
It only shows the upper jaw
C.why: Bitewings show the crowns and bone crest only; the apices and periapical bone are outside the image.

whyNot.0: Dose isn't the issue; the area needed is simply not on the image.
whyNot.2: Bitewings show both the upper and lower jaws.
whyNot.3: The same receptors can be used for bitewings and periapicals.

C.q: For an occlusal radiograph, where is the receptor placed?
options: Against the cheek, outside the mouth
In a holder parallel to one tooth
C.why: An occlusal receptor lies flat between the upper and lower teeth, with the patient biting gently on it.

whyNot.0: Upright behind the molars is not a standard intraoral position.
whyNot.1: Receptors outside the mouth are used for extraoral views.
whyNot.2: A holder parallel to a tooth is the paralleling periapical technique.

C.q: Which of these is NOT a main use of bitewing radiographs?
C.why: Periapical infection needs the apex in view, which bitewings don't show.

whyNot.0: Interproximal caries is the classic bitewing use.
whyNot.1: Overhanging restoration margins show clearly on bitewings.
whyNot.2: Bitewings show the crest of the alveolar bone.

reteach.title: Three cameras, three jobs
reteach.question: If a bitewing, a periapical and an occlusal were three different cameras, what kind of photo would each one take?

blocks.body: A bitewing is a close-up of the 'meeting point' where the upper and lower back teeth bite together, perfect for spotting decay hiding between teeth, but it crops off the roots. A periapical is a full-length portrait of one or two teeth, head (crown) to toe (apex), with the bone around the feet. An occlusal is a wide-angle shot looking down on, or up at, a whole arch, used for things the other two can't fit in, like a stone under the tongue.

blocks.text: Bitewing = BITE on it, both jaws, no roots. Periapical = PERI (around) the APEX, so the root tip must be in the picture.

explain.body: Horizontal bitewings show upper and lower premolar and molar crowns on one image, with no apices. Uses: interproximal caries, recurrent caries, overhangs and the crest of the bone. Vertical bitewings show more bone for periodontal assessment.

explain.caption: Both jaws, crowns only: a bitewing.

test.q: A horizontal bitewing shows which of the following?
options: The crowns of upper and lower back teeth
The full roots of the lower molars
test.why: A horizontal bitewing captures the crowns of the upper and lower posterior teeth together.

whyNot.1: Full roots and apices need a periapical.
whyNot.2: Both whole jaws on one image is a panoramic (DPT).
whyNot.3: The floor of the mouth needs a lower true occlusal.

explain.body: A periapical shows the whole tooth, including the apex and periapical bone. Uses: apical infection, root shape, fractures, before extractions and during root canal treatment. Use the paralleling technique with a holder and beam-aiming device.

test.q: In the paralleling technique, how is the receptor positioned?
options: Parallel to the long axis of the tooth
test.why: The receptor is held in a holder parallel to the tooth's long axis, and the beam is aimed at right angles to both.

whyNot.0: Flat between the teeth is the occlusal position.
whyNot.1: Against the cheek is outside the mouth, as for extraoral views.
whyNot.3: A fixed 45° angle is not part of the paralleling technique.

explain.body: A larger receptor lies flat between the teeth and covers one arch. Upper standard occlusal: anterior maxilla (unerupted canines, supernumeraries). Lower true occlusal: beam up through the floor of the mouth (submandibular duct stones, foreign bodies).

explain.caption: Lower true occlusal: the whole lower arch from below.

test.q: Which finding is an upper standard occlusal commonly used to look for?
test.why: An upper standard occlusal shows the anterior maxilla, where unerupted canines and supernumeraries are found.

whyNot.0: Submandibular stones need the lower true occlusal.
whyNot.2: Interproximal caries is a bitewing job.
whyNot.3: Bone levels are assessed with vertical bitewings or periapicals.

explain.body: Look for two things: how many jaws, and whether the apices show. Both jaws and no apices: bitewing. One jaw, apices showing: periapical. A whole arch seen from above or below: occlusal.

test.q: An image shows two lower molars from crown to root tip with surrounding bone. What type is it?
test.why: One jaw with the whole tooth including the apex is a periapical.

whyNot.0: A bitewing shows both jaws and no apices.
whyNot.1: An occlusal shows the whole arch from below.
whyNot.2: A vertical bitewing still shows both jaws rather than the full root to apex.
